handover14.text: Morning, {called}. A year as Senior Resident. You've stopped flinching at the pager and started flinching at Mr. Malhotra.

then.text: Raju Yadav came for his clinic. Back on the scaffolding, with a belt this time. He asked after you.

else.text: Raju Yadav laid the new wall round the car park. He says it's crooked on purpose, for character.

handover14.text: News. Dr. Sethi got the consultant post. He has a parking space with his name on it. He mentions it.

then.text: He's been polite to you since the apology. Polite Sethi is unsettling. Like a cat that brings you tea.
then.head: tilt

then.text: He still says good morning to everyone except you. It's very precise.

else.text: He calls you 'a resident who doesn't make trouble'. He thinks it's a compliment.

handover14.text: And this is Dr. Zoya Qureshi. Intern. First week. Yours.
Hello! Hi. Sorry. Good morning, Doctor. Dr. Iyer teaches from your admission notes. I've read them twice. I wrote the important bits on my hand.
Check everything she writes. Teach her the way you wanted to be taught. You remember how you wanted to be taught?
One more thing. Orthopaedics is a senior short this month. Dr. Bhatt has borrowed you for tomorrow's hip list. Dr. Rao says it's good for you.
Dr. Rao says that about everything unpleasant.

choose.text: Ask me anything, Zoya. Any time. There are no stupid questions at three in the morning.

then.text: Any time. Even the... okay. I'll be very annoying.
then.head: nod

then.text: She will be. Good.

choose.text: Watch me for a week. Then you do it, and I watch you.

then.text: Watch. Okay. I'm good at watching. It's the doing I'm worried about.
then.head: nod

choose.text: You lead from today. I'll catch you before you fall.

then.text: Catch her early, {called}. Interns fall fast, and quietly.

handover14.text: Priya: Admissions. Eighty-one, fell at home. She wants someone who doesn't whisper.

gomes_arrive.text: Mrs. Philomena Gomes, eighty-one. Fell in the night. Lay on her kitchen floor until the milkman found her at six. Left leg short and turned out.
EH? Is that the doctor? Everybody in this hospital whispers. Is it a hospital or a library?
She keeps asking us to repeat things. Should I do a confusion score?
gomes_arrive.head: tilt

choose.text: Pull up a chair, face her, and speak slowly.

then.text: Mrs. Gomes. I'm {called}. I'm going to sit here, so you can see my face.
Ah. A face. Finally. The young man on the ambulance spoke to my feet.

choose.text: Get the details from Priya, over her head. It's faster.

then.text: I'm down HERE, child. Broken, not furniture.

gomes_arrive.text: Dr. Bhatt wants her on tomorrow's list. Ask her everything you'll need for theatre.

then.text: Much better. Now you can stop shouting. Francis says I'm deaf. I say everybody mumbles.
Oh. She isn't confused at all. She just couldn't hear us.

choose.text: Deaf isn't confused. Check the hearing aid, the glasses and the teeth before you write 'confused' on anyone.

then.text: Hearing aid, glasses, teeth. Writing it down.

choose.text: Write that one on your hand.

then.text: Already did. Both hands.

else.text: What? Speak UP.
She's quite muddled. She didn't answer half the questions. I'll put 'confused' in the notes.
Her son's driving from Pune. He'll know how she usually is.

then.text: Warfarin. So her blood won't clot properly in theatre tomorrow?
then.head: tilt

then.text: Stop it tonight. Vitamin K now. Her clotting checked at six. Put all of it on the chart.
Stop warfarin, vitamin K, clotting at six. On the chart.

else.text: I'll copy her tablets from the GP letter onto the chart tonight. All of them.
All of them, Doctor?
else.head: tilt

then.text: Penicillin allergy. I'll put the red band on her wrist.

gomes_after.text: Will I walk again? My granddaughter gets married in March. I have a blue sari waiting.

choose.text: The operation is your best chance to walk. I can't promise March. I can promise we'll try.

then.text: A doctor who doesn't promise. Good. The last one promised, and here I am on a trolley.
then.head: nod

choose.text: You'll be dancing at that wedding.

then.text: Careful, Doctor. She'll hold you to that.
I will. In the blue sari.

francis_talk.text: Francis Gomes. Her son. Five hours from Pune, and the highway was a car park. Where do I sign? Let's get this done.
Consent forms are for the patient, Mr. Gomes.
She's eighty-one, Sister. She gets confused. Last Sunday on the phone she didn't know what day it was. I'm her son. I'll sign.

choose.text: She isn't confused. She's deaf. With her hearing aid in, she answered every question I asked. She can decide for herself.

then.text: Her hearing aid. She hates it. She says it whistles. ...She answered everything?
then.head: tilt

then.text: Including what she's wearing to your daughter's wedding.
The blue sari. ...Okay. We ask her together. In the morning.
then.head: nod

choose.text: If it makes things easier, sign here.

then.text: Doctor.
Thank you. Finally someone in this hospital who gets things done.

choose.text: Before anyone signs, give me five minutes with her. Properly.

then.title: Five minutes later
then.text: A black hearing aid, at the bottom of her handbag, under a rosary and three sweets.
Now I can hear. Francis? You drove all this way! Did you eat anything?
...She isn't confused.
then.head: down

then.text: She's deaf, Mr. Gomes. Deaf people get called confused in hospitals every day. That's our fault, not theirs.

choose.text: You know her best. Sign here.

then.text: Nobody asked her, Doctor.

francis_talk.text: Should she even have an operation at her age? Isn't it safer to let it heal on its own?
francis_talk.head: tilt

choose.text: A hip like hers doesn't heal in bed. In bed, old people get pneumonia, clots and sores. The operation is how she gets up again, and soon is safer than late.

then.text: So the safe thing is the frightening thing. ...That's every decision with my mother.
then.head: down

choose.text: Dr. Bhatt will explain it all tomorrow.

then.text: Everyone here will explain tomorrow.

francis_talk.text: I phone on Sundays. Mostly. She lay on that floor for five hours.
francis_talk.head: down

francis_talk.text: She's here now. Go and sit with her. The chair by her bed is terrible. You'll fit right in.

morning15.text: Morning. I wrote Mrs. Gomes's drug chart at three, after the second admission. And a stomach ache. And a man who swallowed a key.
Check it together before the drug round. Teach, don't fix. Fix it for her and she makes the same mistake on someone else next Tuesday at three.

then.text: I copied her tablets from the GP letter exactly. So that part's definitely right.
then.head: nod

morning15.text: Tell me what's wrong. Be nice about it. Or don't. Whichever works.

then.text: Every one. And you never doubted the lines I got right. I'm making a list of what you checked, so I can check it myself.
And her warfarin? Still on the chart. Nobody gave the vitamin K. Her clotting this morning is 2.8. Theatre needs to know.
That's mine. I copied it straight across.
then.head: down

else.text: The pharmacist caught what you two missed. That's why we have pharmacists. Don't make a habit of needing them.

choose.text: Everyone makes these at three in the morning. That's why we check each other. You did the right thing asking.

then.text: I thought you'd shout. A surgeon at my medical college threw a chart once.
then.head: tilt

then.text: We don't throw charts here. We file them.

choose.text: These are the mistakes that kill people. Slow down at three in the morning, or call me.

then.text: Slow down, or call you. ...Yes. Sorry.
then.head: nod

choose.text: We'll fill in an incident form together. Not to blame you: so the hospital learns why charts written at three go wrong.

then.text: An incident form. With my name on it?
With the time on it. Three in the morning is the problem, not you.
Good. Mr. Malhotra will hate it. That's how you know it's useful.
then.head: nod

chart_after.text: Mrs. Gomes is first on Dr. Bhatt's list. He's already asking where his borrowed surgeon is.

gomes_consent.text: Ah, my doctor with the face. Francis says I'm having an operation. Am I? Nobody has told me.
gomes_consent.head: tilt

then.text: Francis says he signed a paper for me. For MY hip. As if I'm a cupboard he's moving house.
Mummy, you couldn't hear anyone, they said you were...
Then someone should have found my hearing aid! It's in my handbag! It has always been in my handbag!

choose.text: You're right. I should have asked you. Let me explain it now, and you decide. Your signature, not his.

then.text: Better. Explain slowly. I taught Portuguese for forty years. I know when someone skips a page.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Your son has signed, so we're fine to go ahead.

then.text: Fine for you.
then.head: down

then.text: Mummy...
then.head: down

else.text: Francis says you told him I can decide for myself. Nobody has said that to me since my husband died.

then.text: A cut on the side of your thigh. A big screw up the neck of the bone, and a plate along the side. You'll be awake, but numb from the waist down.
The risks: bleeding, infection, clots in the legs, and in soft old bone the screw can slip and need doing again.
And if I say no?
then.head: tilt

then.text: Then months in bed. And bed is dangerous at eighty-one.
Then yes. Give me the pen. Not the cheap one.

gomes_consent.text: One thing. My hearing aid stays in. I want to hear what you say about my bones.

hip_brief.text: Ah! General surgery's finest, on loan. Welcome to the bone room. Drills, hammers, X-rays. Very relaxing.
Spinal's working. She's awake behind the screen, and she's told me about every saint in Margao.
The plan: a guide wire under X-ray, a screw up the neck along the wire, a plate on the side. Read both X-ray views. Bones lie from one angle.

then.text: Her clotting's 2.8 this morning. Somebody never stopped her warfarin. I've given vitamin K, but it's slow. Expect her to bleed.
Lovely. Pressure on everything, then.

else.text: Clotting's 1.4. Whoever stopped her warfarin in time: thank you.
else.head: nod

hip_brief.text: Time-out first, Doctor. I'll read the board.

then.text: Fixed. I finished it. Her bone was soft as cake. It happens, at eighty-one.

choose.text: It got away from me. Dr. Bhatt took over, and it's done well.

then.text: Honest and alive. Both good things in a doctor.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Her bone was very soft.

then.text: It was. And you'll learn soft bone. Say that bit too.
Screw dead centre, plate flat. You can borrow my drill any time, Doctor.

else.text: Fixed. It took a while. Her bones forgave us.

then.text: She bled. Two units. Her warfarin was never stopped. That's a chart problem, not a bone problem.

else.text: She bled more than I like. One unit. She's pink again.

then.text: And next time, the wire stays out of the joint. I nudged it back.

gomes_after_op.text: Tomorrow. With a frame, and a physiotherapist who has no mercy.
Good. Mercy is for people with time.
gomes_after_op.head: nod

then.text: And thank you for making me ask her. I'd forgotten I was allowed to.
then.head: down

gomes_after_op.text: She lives alone. Who's going to be with her when she goes home?

choose.text: That's for you and your mother to decide together. I'll ask the physio and the social worker to help you both.

then.text: Together. Listen to that, Francis. Together.

choose.text: She shouldn't be alone at first. Can you stay a few weeks, or can she come to Pune?

then.text: Pune! Traffic, and people in a hurry.
...We'll talk about it, Mummy.
then.head: nod

budget_preview.text: Doctor! Five minutes. On Thursday the budget committee votes. One big item for surgery. Two choices.
Choice A: a surgical robot. Patients from three districts. Our name in the newspaper. Look, the brochure has a smiling grandmother.
Choice B: a second doctor at night, so the senior resident isn't alone with the whole floor. Very worthy. Nobody puts a night doctor in a newspaper.
Dr. Sethi wants the robot. Dr. Iyer wants the doctor. Dr. Rao chairs and won't say. Which leaves you with the deciding vote. Congratulations.

choose.text: I've done nights alone. One doctor for forty patients is how people get missed.

then.text: Spoken like someone who's tired. Do tomorrow night first. Then tell me.

choose.text: The robot brings patients, and patients bring money for everything else.

then.text: Finally. Someone who reads to page forty.

choose.text: I'll decide after my night shift.

then.text: A night shift as research. Very scientific.

budget_preview.text: Tomorrow night you're in charge of the floor. Count how many more doctors you wish you had. Or robots.

night16.text: Evening. I'm the consultant on call tonight. From home. I have a parking space now. Did Grace tell you?

then.text: You and I have had our moments. Tonight none of that matters. Call me if you need me.
We're past last year. I meant that apology. Call me if you need me.
then.head: nod

else.text: You've never made trouble. Don't start at three in the morning.

night16.text: My patient in bed five, Mr. Nanda. Two days ago I took out a piece of his bowel and joined the ends. He's sore. Sore is normal. Don't call me for sore.
He was a bit fast at eight. Pulse ninety.
night16.head: tilt

night16.text: Fast because he's sore. Paracetamol. Good night, everyone.
So it's just us. Forty patients, one of you, one of me. And Priya.

choose.text: We'll do the ten o'clock round together, bed by bed. Then you'll know what I look for.

then.text: Together. Okay. I'll bring the charts. Checked ones.
then.head: nod

choose.text: You take the round, Zoya. I'll be in admissions. Call me if anything worries you.

then.text: Anything. Any time. You said.
then.head: nod

else.text: Only if it's really bad, though. I don't want to waste your time.
else.head: down

night16.text: Coffee's in the cupboard. Don't drink the one marked 'Sister Grace'. Nobody survives that.

then.text: His pulse was ninety at eight. It's a hundred and twelve now. Dr. Sethi said sore is normal, but you said any time.

else.text: I've watched him since ten. His pulse kept going up. Dr. Sethi said not to call about sore, and I didn't want to waste your time.
else.head: down

choose.text: Next time, call me the first time something worries you. Wasting my time is my job.

then.text: Wasting your time is your job. ...That's going on my hand.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Two and a half hours, Zoya?

then.text: I know. I know.
then.head: down

nanda_round.text: Just sore, Doctor. Dr. Sethi said sore is normal. Is sore supposed to move about like this?

then.text: A leak? From the join? That's bad, isn't it?

else.text: So it isn't a leak? Good. I read about leaks. They scared me.
else.head: tilt

nanda_call.text: Is it bad, Doctor? My daughter's coming from Nagpur tomorrow.
nanda_call.head: tilt

choose.text: Phone Dr. Sethi. Now.

then.text: It's midnight. Is this about sore?
His pulse went from 88 to 112, temperature 38.4, his belly is rigid, and he's made forty millilitres of urine in four hours. I think the join is leaking.
...Rigid. Right. Book theatre. I'm twenty minutes away. And {called}? Thank you for not listening to me.
then.head: nod

else.text: His pulse is 112 and his belly's tender. I'm not sure why.
Not sure? Fine. Nothing by mouth, fluids, bloods. I'm coming in to look. Next time, know what you think before you call.

then.text: He's coming. He's actually coming.

choose.text: Fluids, bloods, and I'll see him again in an hour.

then.text: An hour. Okay. I'll set an alarm.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It's pain. Morphine, and let him sleep.

then.text: Morphine. Thank God.
then.head: down

then.text: ...Morphine. Okay.
then.head: down

imran_arrive.text: Imran Ali, twenty-four. Fell two floors from the scaffolding at the new mall. His friends carried him in on a door.
No harness. The contractor said harnesses slow the work.
imran_arrive.head: down

imran_arrive.text: His friends are outside. One of them is crying.

then.text: Dr. Sethi's still here, closing Mr. Nanda in Theatre 2. He'll come straight across.

else.text: Dr. Sethi's at home. Twenty minutes at night, if the railway gates are up.

choose.text: Zoya, ask his friends: allergies, medicines, when he last ate. Quickly.

then.text: No allergies. No medicines. Rice at seven. And his wife is on her way.

choose.text: Everyone hands on. Questions later.

then.text: Hands on. Fine.
then.head: nod

imran_arrive.text: Examine him, Doctor. I'll call out his numbers.

then.text: His spleen. Then he needs a theatre, not a scanner.
then.head: nod

else.text: He's getting paler, Doctor. Whatever it is, it's bleeding.

choose.text: Straight to theatre. He's too unstable for the scanner.

then.text: Theatre 1 is ready. Dr. Khan's on her way up.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Get a CT scan first. I want to know exactly what's broken.

then.title: Twenty-five minutes later
then.text: In the scanner his pressure fell to seventy. The scan shows a burst spleen. Everyone already knew.

imran_plan.text: Who watches the ward while you're in theatre? Mr. Nanda...

choose.text: You hold the ward, Zoya, with Priya. If anyone worries you, Mr. Nanda included, call Dr. Sethi yourself. Don't wait for me.

then.text: Call the consultant. Myself. ...Okay. I can do that. I can definitely do that.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Scrub in with me, Zoya. You've never seen a belly opened in a hurry. Priya holds the ward.

then.text: Priya holds forty patients. Alone. Again. Lovely.

imran_ready.text: Theatre 1. Blood's running through the warmer. Go.
Doctor. Tell Rubina I'm sorry about the harness.
imran_ready.head: down

then.text: Two in one night. Mr. Nanda's join was leaking, as you said. Washed out and stable. Now this one.

else.text: Twenty minutes. The railway gates were down. What have we got?

spleen_brief.text: Two units in, pressure eighty-five. A thin boy who's lost a lot of blood. Be quick, and be kind to my numbers.

then.text: And next time, a bleeding patient does not go into the scanner. They call it the doughnut of death for a reason.

spleen_brief.text: Your hands, my eyes, {called}. If you're wrong, I'll tell you quietly. I've learnt that much this year.
spleen_brief.head: nod

spleen_brief.text: Time-out. The fast version, but all of it.

then.text: He's alive. I finished it. Nights like this, everybody's hands shake. Mine too.
Clean, at three in the morning. I've seen consultants do worse. I've been one.
then.head: nod

else.text: He's alive. It was untidy. We'll talk about it in daylight.

then.text: No spleen. He needs vaccines, and antibiotics for any fever, for the rest of his life. Write it big in the notes.
He keeps his spleen. At twenty-four, that matters for fifty years.
then.head: nod

then.text: And his pancreas will sulk for a week. We'll watch the drain.
Zoya phoned Dr. Sethi at half past three. About Mr. Nanda. She said you told her to.
She did. I took him to theatre between your case and dawn. Leaking like a tap. He's in intensive care. He'll live.
Your intern made the call that should have been made at midnight.
then.head: tilt

choose.text: She did. I didn't. I'll say so tomorrow.

then.text: So will I. I told you all not to call me for sore.
then.head: down

choose.text: You told us not to call you for sore.

then.text: ...I did say that. Didn't I.
then.head: down

imran_after.text: Go and lie down for an hour. You won't sleep. Nobody does.

then.text: They say I had a second operation. I don't remember agreeing. I remember the young doctor's face. She looked scared for me.
then.head: tilt

then.text: I was.
then.head: nod

then.text: By morning he'd have been septic. You called me at midnight. That's the whole story. Remember it for the M&M: sometimes it's about what went right.
He's in intensive care, on oxygen, sitting up and complaining about the food. That's a good sign.
I nearly didn't call. I kept hearing 'don't call for sore'.
then.head: down

else.text: Priya found him grey at half past five. Pressure sixty. Septic. I took him to theatre at six. He's on a ventilator in intensive care.
else.head: down

else.text: I should have called. I watched his pulse go up all night and I wrote it down very neatly.
else.head: down

else.text: And I told everyone not to call me for sore. We'll talk about that at the M&M. All of us.

choose.text: Thank you for coming in, Dr. Sethi.

then.text: Coming in is the job. Saying 'call me' and meaning it is the job too. I'm learning that late.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Zoya, go home and sleep. You did a lot tonight.

then.text: I don't think I can sleep. But I'll lie down and stare at the ceiling. Professionally.

imran_visit.text: Rubina. His wife. They told me he fell, and that he nearly died. Nobody has told me what happened in between.
Tell her the boring parts too, Doctor. She likes details. She's an accountant.

choose.text: His spleen burst in the fall. Let me tell you exactly what we did, and what it means now.

then.text: We took his spleen out. He can live well without it, but infections hit him harder now. Vaccines this month, and a doctor quickly for any fever. For life.
For life. I'll write it in my diary. In red.

else.text: We stitched a tear in his spleen and kept it. Six weeks with no lifting, and come straight back if the pain gets worse.
Six weeks. The contractor will love that.

choose.text: The operation went well. He'll be fine.

then.text: Fine. Everyone says fine. Fine is not a medical word.

imran_visit.text: The contractor came at seven with fruit and a paper. He wants Imran to sign that he fell at home. Then there's no compensation, and no case.
If I don't sign, he won't hire me again. If I sign, who pays for this?
imran_visit.head: down

choose.text: I'll write what happened in his notes: a fall from scaffolding, at work, with no harness. What you sign is your choice. The notes won't lie.

then.text: Write it. With the time.
then.head: nod

choose.text: That's between you and the contractor.

then.text: Of course. Everyone stays out of it. That's how he keeps doing it.
then.head: down

mm.text: Morbidity and mortality. The rules: we talk about what went wrong, not about whom to hang. Dr. Qureshi.
Mr. Harish Nanda, fifty-eight. A piece of bowel removed by Dr. Sethi, day two. At eight in the evening his pulse was ninety. At ten, a hundred and four.

then.text: At eleven, a hundred and twelve. I called my senior. My senior phoned Dr. Sethi at midnight. Theatre by one. A small leak, washed out. He's back on the ward.
A near miss, caught. Good. Who noticed first?
then.head: tilt

choose.text: Dr. Qureshi did. She saw his pulse climbing and she called me. I picked up the phone.

then.text: Oh.
I remember a meeting in this room where I did the opposite. Point taken.
then.head: down

else.text: Credit where it's due. Noted.
else.head: nod

choose.text: I caught it on my round, and I called Dr. Sethi.

then.text: ...Yes.
then.head: down

then.text: Hm.
I watched him until half past twelve, then he was seen. Then a trauma came in. I phoned Dr. Sethi myself at half past three. Theatre at four. Intensive care. Alive.

else.text: I watched him until half past twelve before anyone was told. Then a trauma came in. Nobody saw him again until half past five. Septic shock. Theatre at six. He's still on a ventilator.
else.head: down

else.text: So. Why did it take so long?

choose.text: Because we were told not to call for sore. A consultant said it, and an intern believed him. That isn't her fault. It's how we talk to juniors.

then.text: Here we go again.
Kabir.
then.head: tilt

then.text: ...No. They're right. I said it. I've said it for ten years.
then.head: down

else.text: I said that. I've said it for ten years. It sounded clever.
else.head: down

choose.text: Because I didn't go and look at him myself. I was in charge of the floor. That's mine.

then.text: Honest. Not the whole story, though. Dr. Sethi?
then.head: tilt

then.text: I told them not to call me for sore. That's the rest of it.
then.head: down

choose.text: The intern should have called earlier.

then.text: She has been a doctor for nine days, {called}. Who taught her what to call about?

mm.text: Actions. One: any doctor can call any consultant at any hour, and nobody says 'sore'. Two: a rising pulse after a bowel join is a leak until proven otherwise.
Write it on the wall. Write it on your hand, Dr. Qureshi. I've seen you do it.

vote.text: The budget. One item, two options. A: the robot. B: a second doctor at night. Dr. Sethi?

then.text: The robot. It brings patients from three districts. We'd be the only one between here and Nagpur.

else.text: The robot. ...Although, after this week, I'll say robot quietly.
else.head: down

vote.text: The doctor. I did nights alone for twenty years. So did everyone at this table. That isn't a tradition. It's a risk.
Bones don't care about robots. I abstain. Unless the robot can make tea.
I chair. I don't vote. {called}, you were alone with the floor on Tuesday night. You decide it.

then.text: You said the robot, Doctor. Page forty.
You said the night doctor. That was before your night. And now?
then.head: tilt

choose.text: A second doctor at night. On Tuesday I had a leaking bowel and a burst spleen at the same time, and a nine-day intern holding the ward.

then.text: The robot brochure had a smiling grandmother.
Then hire a smiling night doctor, Vikram.

choose.text: The robot. Patients travel for it, and the money it brings will help everything else, nights included.

then.text: Then come and do my nights with the robot, {called}.
Wonderful! I'll call the photographer.
Mrs. Gomes walked to the window with a frame. Slowly. She said 'March' to the physiotherapist twice.

else.text: Mrs. Gomes walked the length of the ward with a frame and told the physiotherapist he has no rhythm.

then.text: She left you a card. 'For the doctor who let me sign my own name.' In Portuguese, then English, then Portuguese again to be sure.

else.text: She asked me to tell you she's still cross with you. Then she gave me a sweet for you anyway.

then.text: The labour inspector came for Imran's notes. The contractor is paying the hospital bill. And buying harnesses. Thirty of them.

else.text: Imran signed the contractor's paper. He'll be back on the scaffold in six weeks. No harness.
else.head: down

then.text: Mr. Nanda is off the ventilator. He asked for his daughter, then for idli. In that order.

else.text: Mr. Nanda goes home this morning. He shook Zoya's hand for a full minute.

then.text: And the night nurses heard about the vote. They've put your name on the coffee cupboard. It's an honour. Don't drink from it.

else.text: And someone has drawn a moustache on the grandmother in the robot brochure. Not me. Probably not me.

then.text: Good luck at your review, Doctor.
then.head: down

then.text: You said there are no stupid questions at three in the morning. I asked eleven this week. Thank you for answering all of them.

else.text: Thank you for checking my chart. I check everyone's now. People hate it.

choose.text: You'll be better at this than me, Zoya.

then.text: That's what Dr. Iyer said about you. I asked her.

choose.text: Keep writing on your hands.

then.text: I've run out of hand. I've started on my arm.

letters18.text: Review at three. Seminar room. Clean coat. You know the drill.

review_surgeon.text: Sit, {called}. A year as Senior Resident. Dr. Bhatt borrowed you, so he speaks first.

then.text: Clean hands, careful with the X-ray. If general surgery ever bores you, there's a drill with your name on it.
A hard bone on a hard day, and the sense to let go before it got worse. That's half of orthopaedics.

else.text: She walks. That's the review.

then.text: And an eighty-one-year-old signed her own form. Do you know how rare that is on my ward? Rarer than a straight femur.
The incident form about the three a.m. charts: pharmacy has changed the night drug round because of it.
At the M&M you gave your intern the credit. In this room last year, someone took yours. You remembered which side of that you want to be on.
then.head: nod

then.text: Your intern noticed Mr. Nanda first, and you let the room think it was you. I've seen where that habit goes. So have you.
You blamed a nine-day intern in front of the department. That's the one thing from this year I won't forget.
And you said out loud why nobody calls at night. It took a consultant ten years to hear it. It took you one sentence.
Tuesday night: two emergencies, both alive, and a consultant called at midnight because you trusted your hands over his words.
Tuesday night: you told your intern to make the call, and she made it. Next time, make it yourself at midnight.

else.text: Tuesday night: Mr. Nanda nearly died, and you know when it could have been different. Good. A surgeon who doesn't carry one patient around is dangerous.
else.head: down

then.text: And a burst spleen at three in the morning, done properly.
then.head: nod

then.text: You cost me a robot, Doctor. The board asked me to find the money for a night doctor. ...I found it. Don't tell anyone how easily.

else.text: The robot arrives in April. You're first on the training list. The brochure needs a young surgeon.

review_surgeon.text: Surgeon, {called}. Your own patients. Your own operating list. Your name on the board outside theatre, and nobody's hands over yours.

choose.text: Thank you. Dr. Iyer, for every time you kept your hands in your pockets.

then.text: Now keep yours in yours. Your intern is watching.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I made enough mistakes this year to fill an M&M.

then.text: Then one day you'll chair a good one.
then.head: nod

choose.text: When do I get a parking space?

then.text: There's a waiting list. Dr. Sethi is on it twice.

review_surgeon.text: Surgeon. Which means you're the one people call now. Congratulations, Doctor.
